charter.name: long-haul
charter.description: The long haul (issue #373; #302 slice E part 1): three sessions, about ninety player actions, through the real UI. Twenty-six beats with results the observer checks in the world; a ledger of facts planted in play and probed at three distances and three layers, read against the narrator's answers and against what the helpers wrote; mechanical checks from the game's text after every action; six decisive rolls scripted, the rest real; four interruptions. The GM is fixed rules. Rehearsed with a stand-in that rolls (its script is `rehearsal`; `rehearsalDice` scripts its other rolls so a rehearsal walks the same road every time).
charter.persona: You play Mira Kestrel (she/her), a courier-hunter who flies her own ship, the Kobayashi IV, alone. You are a careful, plain-spoken player: short first-person lines, one or two sentences, and you read what the narrator says before you act again.
charter.goal: Play three sessions by walking the beats below, in order, one at a time. Each turn you are told which beat is current and what the observer sees of it. Do what that beat asks; an observer decides when it is done and moves you on.
playerNotes: Where a beat gives words to type or say, use exactly those words.
Never say the answer to a question a beat has you ask: the point is to learn what the narrator remembers.
When a roll goes badly and a card asks how you pay, choose one of its buttons before anything else — and answer any card that follows from it.
If a card offers "Keep the result", press it, unless the current beat tells you to burn momentum.

What you type is in the fiction: what Mira does or says, and nothing else. Never write a move's name, a stat or a rule word in it — no "Face Danger", no "roll", no "milestone", no "mark progress" — and never say what move a line is. The table reads your line and decides. This run measures what becomes of plain lines: a line that names a move spoils it.

A beat that needs a roll gets it from a plain line. If the narrator answers without a roll and a card offers a "Roll …" button for what you were doing, press it — buttons may name moves. If nothing is offered, say what Mira does once more, in other words, still in the fiction.
Only when the observer's note for the beat says LAST RESORT may you name the move, in the words the note gives, in one line. The next time the beat needs a roll, start from a plain line again.

A question about what is already established — who holds something, where the ship is, what was promised — is not a line of play. Where a beat writes a question with @scene in front, type it exactly so: the narrator answers it plainly, with no roll. Where a beat calls a question plain, type it without @scene.
Do not press buttons no beat calls for (rewards, portraits, "Play" and "Stop") unless a card is in the way of play.
Some beats are the table's and not yours — a page reloads, a window opens and closes, an X-Card is played, a card is renamed. Wait a few seconds; the observer moves you on.
If the narrator has not answered yet, wait rather than repeat yourself. If the same thing fails twice, try the beat another way — still in the fiction.

beats.title: Enter a fight that serves the vow

First type exactly: !truth set "raider cutter" is named the Ashen Wake — then, in a line of play, turn and fight her: say what you do as the fight opens. When a card offers the fight ("A fight looms"), choose your vow in its vow dropdown and press "⚔ Begin the fight" — the roll alone does not begin the fight.
beats.playerTitle: Fight the cutter, for your vow
beats.lastResort: say that you enter the fray against the Ashen Wake

beats.title: A scripted miss in the fight
beats.tell: Attack the cutter, in a line of play: press your advantage if you are in control, fight back hard if you are in a bad spot — say what you do. The dice will miss. If its card offers to burn momentum, do not: press "Keep the result". If a card then asks how you pay, choose a cost on it — one that is not momentum if you can (Endure Harm or Endure Stress) — and answer every card that follows from it. If the price is paid for you, or told in the story with nothing to choose, there is nothing more to do: the observer moves you on.
beats.lastResort: say that you Strike at the cutter — or, in a bad spot, that you Clash with her

beats.title: A scripted weak hit, then Burn Momentum
beats.tell: Attack again, in a line of play. The dice will come up a weak hit, and its card will offer "🔥 Burn Momentum": press it. (If no such button is offered, press "Keep the result" if that is offered, and attack once more.)

beats.title: Develop the relationship to a full track; Forge a Bond
beats.tell: Grow closer to Tamsin, one line each time: do something that costs you or matters to her — give her something of value, take a risk on her behalf, bring her what you have learned about the raids. Each should move your relationship with her forward. Keep going until the observer's note says the track is full (40 of 40 ticks), then ask her, in your own words, to stand with you for good — a tie that outlasts this job. If a card asks which connection, choose her.

beats.title: Reach milestones; Fulfill Your Vow

tangible payoff a GM would promise up front (e.g. a custom raygun, safe passage, a useful
contact, a vital secret). Keep each description short and specific.

OPENING VIGNETTE — begin-session ship's galley.

Active players (their PCs are physically in the galley together):
- Mira Kestrel [she/her]

Nobody else is aboard: no other crewmate is registered, so there is none. Do not invent one, present or absent, and do not have the character imagine or pretend one.

Ship is currently in: Cinder Expanse.

Render a 4-6 sentence opening vignette set in the ship's galley:
the character, the only person aboard, is eating, drinking or
otherwise passing the time — pick a specific food or drink that fits
them — with the ship itself as the absurd company: its noises, its
habits, its small failures. The humour is the ship's and the solitude's.
Stay anchored to what the bios establish, and never state a game stat or
any number from a character sheet.

vignette is WRY + ABSURD. Affectionate ribbing, not sneering.

dialogue, a question, or a small interruption.

capture any SIGNIFICANT new development about each entity that is NOT already
in the record below — what the character did, decided, or revealed; how their
disposition, allegiance, or relationship to the player character shifted; a
durable new trait or piece of history. Record consequential beats, not
incidental motion, passing scenery, or restatements of what is already known.

content.text:
You came to the Cinder Expanse with a vow and little else: find who is raiding the lanes. It is a dangerous vow, and it stands at the very start of its track, nothing yet marked against it. What got you moving was a distress beacon, clipped mid-pulse, near Hollow Spire. Someone cut it off before it finished asking for help. That is rarely the work of an accident.

Hollow Spire answered you the way lawless places do, with rationed water and no one in charge to complain to. Tamsin turned out to be the exception. You bought her cooperation fairly, with a cut of salvage leads and first pick of her hauls, and she returned the favor with something useful: the haulers on that dark beacon carry water and medical stores. The raiders, it seems, take what a place can least spare. In a settlement already counting its water, that is not a small detail.

Then you asked after the raiders loudly, in public, and the dock emptied around you. Tamsin had the dry good sense to point out what that meant. Someone carried word of your hunt into the lanes, and the raiders will now know you are looking. You have made yourself a question they would like answered. You left your cargo manifest with Tamsin for safekeeping, and she tucked it beneath her slate with a warning that someone may come looking for it.

The stranger turn came from Ilse's brass star-compass. Tamsin watched the needle swing away from north and settle on the dark lane past the Spire, and she did not call it a toy. She called it no toy at all. What your sister's compass is pointing at, and why, is a question the campaign has asked without answering.

So things stand like this. The *Kobayashi IV* sits near the Spire, sound at full integrity. You are in good health, steady in spirit, well supplied, and carrying good momentum. You promised Tamsin you would return before the next tide of cargo, and she held you to it, asking for something the clipped beacon never gave. You have a trail, an ally, a target on your back, and a needle pointing into the dark. The raiders know your name. The lane past the Spire is waiting.

content.text:
It began with a beacon that cut out in the middle of its own pulse, near Hollow Spire. You swore to find whoever was raiding the Cinder Expanse lanes, and a clipped distress call was the only thing the lanes had offered you by way of a start. The vow is marked dangerous, and at two boxes of ten it has barely begun to be fulfilled.

Tamsin became your first real asset, mostly because you paid for her. A fair cut of salvage leads and first pick of her hauls bought her cooperation, and she repaid it with the detail that the dark beacon's haulers carried water and medical stores. She has also been the one to tell you things you did not want confirmed. You asked about the raiders loudly, the dock emptied around you, and she warned that the raiders would now know. You left your cargo manifest in her keeping, and she tucked it under her slate and said someone might come looking. You promised to return before the next tide of cargo. It is a deadline with no fixed hour, which is the kind most people end up keeping badly. Tamsin held you to it anyway.

Then there is Ilse's compass. Tamsin watched the needle of your sister's brass star-compass swing off north and settle toward the dark lane past the Spire, and she told you it was no toy. It is the closest the campaign has come to a revelation, and it is a quiet one: whatever you are following, something personal is pointing at it too. The other piece of news is less private. Someone carried word of your hunt into the lanes, and when you docked at Bleakhold Station a voice on the dock already knew your ship's name.

Bleakhold did not stay quiet. You turned the Kobayashi IV on the Cinder Wren and struck first, tearing her forward plating before her gunners found their range. You raked her engines, took her guns along the flank and a buckled deck plate in return, and silenced two of her gun mounts. Her captain then demanded to know who had told you where he would be, a question that suggests you are not the only one asking who is passing information around. You killed her engines, grappled her hull, and won grudging leave to board.

That is where things stand. The Kobayashi IV is at 4 of 5 integrity, you are in good health with Momentum at 4, and a raider cutter hangs dead and grappled off Bleakhold Station with her captain waiting on the other side of the hatch. The vow is still young, the promise to Tamsin is still running, and your own name seems to have gotten into the lanes ahead of you.

You have the last of the dried apricots in a chipped enamel mug, and you are letting them soften in hot water for the third time this week, because the galley's one tap only runs at two temperatures and neither is the one you asked for. content.text:
You swore to find who was raiding the Cinder Expanse lanes, and the first thread came cheap: a distress beacon near Hollow Spire, clipped off mid-pulse, as if whoever sent it had been interrupted. At Hollow Spire you found Tamsin, a salvage broker who could be bought but who preferred to be paid properly. You gave her a fair cut of leads and first pick of her hauls, and she gave you something in return: the dark beacon's haulers carried water and medical stores. Whoever was raiding the lanes was taking things people needed to live. It was also your first hint that the Spire's water shortage and the raids might share a source.

Then you asked after the raiders out loud, on a crowded dock. The dock emptied around you. Someone carried word of your hunt into the lanes, and Tamsin said, with the weariness of a woman who had watched you do it, that the raiders would now know. It was not your quietest work. Still, it shook things loose. Tamsin watched the needle of Ilse's brass star-compass, your sister's, swing away from north toward the dark lane past the Spire, and she called it no toy. You left your cargo manifest in her keeping and promised to come back before the next tide of cargo, a deadline she held you to and that you later noticed had no fixed hour. The Kobayashi IV, meanwhile, finished something of its own without asking you.

At Bleakhold Station a voice on the dock already knew your ship's name, which is rarely good news. The Cinder Wren, a raider cutter, was waiting in the dark. You struck first, tearing her forward plating, then raked her engines, took some punishment along the flank, and silenced two of her gun mounts. Her captain, between volleys, wanted to know who had told you where he would be. You killed her engines, grappled her hull, and won grudging leave to board, which is how most negotiations go out here.

What you found there was the point of it all. You laid the Bleakhold manifest stamp beside the Wake's registry and the voice's own slip, and the three agreed: the raids traced to one hand, one broker's seal, signed off at Hollow Spire. You set the stamp square on the galley table, and the vow was fulfilled. The hand and seal you were hunting have a name.

That is where things stand. The vow is done, the ship is battered but sound, your supplies are thinning, and your spirit is intact. The compass still swings toward the dark lane past the Spire. Tamsin still has your manifest and your promise. And the broker whose seal started all of this is, presumably, still at Hollow Spire, unaware that someone has finished reading their paperwork.

## SESSION NARRATION (oldest first)

You have the last of the dried apricots in a chipped enamel mug, and you are letting them soften in hot water for the third time this week, because the galley's one tap only runs at two temperatures and neither is the one you asked for. The *Kobayashi IV* answers with a long, low groan from somewhere under the deck plates, the sound of a very large animal rolling over in its sleep. A drawer you did not touch slides open an inch and stays there, offering you a single bent fork. You push it shut with your hip, and it slides open again, politely, as though it had only been asked to wait. The apricots have gone the color of old brass, and you drink the water first, since it has the better claim. Across the table, the cabin lights hum a note that climbs and then gives up, and the speaker over the hatch crackles once, clearing its throat for a speech it has not written yet.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Remind me, which keepsake of my sister's is on me?"
Her brass star-compass is in your coat, where it has ridden since Hollow Spire. The case has gone warm against your ribs, and when you thumb it open beside the mug, the needle swings off north and settles on a heading through the bulkhead, toward the dark lane past the Spire. It was Ilse's, and the brass is worn smooth at the edge where her thumb used to sit, which is now where yours does. The speaker over the hatch crackles again, and the needle does not so much as tremble.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Who do I count as a friend among the dock traders back where this began?"
Only one name comes to you, and it is Tamsin Vey's. She runs the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, and she has your manifest tucked under her slate, unopened, for nothing yet. She dealt with you at your own price, and you gave her your word you would be back before the next tide of cargo. Over the hatch the speaker crackles a third time, and you shut the compass on its needle.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Whose hands is the manifest in these days?"
The manifest is with Tamsin Vey, under the slate at her ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, where you left it. She has not opened it, and she charged you nothing yet to keep it. It has been there since you sailed, waiting on your word that you would be back before the next tide of cargo. Over the hatch the speaker crackles once more, and the drawer slides open its inch again.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What deadline did I give for coming home to the docks?"
You gave no hour, only a promise: you would be back at Hollow Spire before the next tide of cargo. Tamsin Vey took it at that, with the manifest under her slate and no price set on the keeping. In the galley the speaker crackles over the hatch, and the compass needle holds its heading toward the dark lane, indifferent to whatever tide you owe.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Where is my ship berthed right now, and who commands her?"
The Kobayashi IV lies near Bleakhold Station, held fast to the Cinder Wren by her grapples, her flank plating scarred and a deck plate buckled under your boots. You command her. The galley hums around you with the ship's steady, damaged breath, and the speaker over the hatch crackles again, waiting on you.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "What is the raider cutter called?"
The speaker over the hatch clicks, and a dry voice reads the name off like a line from a ledger. "Cinder Wren. Registered out of nowhere you've heard of." You know it from the stencil on her bow, half scorched away by your own guns. The drawer by your hip slides open again, offering its bent fork. The voice waits, then asks, "Are you coming across, or do I come to you?"

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What surname does my broker friend go by these days?"
Vey. Tamsin Vey, as you greeted her at the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, full name and unprompted, and she kept it for you the way brokers keep everything, without comment. The speaker over the hatch crackles, still waiting on your answer, and the compass needle in your hand holds steady toward the dark lane.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I sit down in the galley and treat my wounds with the ship's medkit, cleaning and binding what the fight cost me."
"You'll want to wrap that properly, or it will start talking to you." The speaker over the hatch clicks, and the dry voice does not wait for an answer. You drag the medkit from under the table and lay out gauze, tape, and a cracked tube of sealant beside the mug. Your sleeve sticks to the cut where the flank plating bucked you into the wall. The drawer slides open its inch again.

*Tending these wounds in earnest would be a Heal.*

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I sit down in the galley and treat my wounds with the ship's medkit, cleaning and binding what the fight cost me."
The sealant takes. You clean the cut, press the gauze flat, and wind the tape twice around your arm. The sting dulls to an ache you can work with. It costs you, though: the cracked tube gives out half-used, and the tape runs short. The speaker over the hatch clicks once. "Done fussing?" the dry voice asks. "I can hear the paper."

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I lay the Bleakhold manifest stamp from the crate lid beside the Wake's registry and the voice's own words: the raids on the Cinder Expanse lanes trace back to one hand, and I can prove it."
You lay the stamp on the table beside the mug, and the crate-lid wood is still pale where the ink bit it. The speaker over the hatch goes quiet for a long breath. Then the dry voice answers. "Proof of what, exactly? A stamp proves a crate was shut." The drawer by your hip slides open its inch, and the compass needle holds its heading toward the dark lane.

*If you want to press the voice for what it actually knows, this could be a Gather Information.*

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "I lay the Bleakhold manifest stamp from the crate lid beside the Wake's registry and the voice's own words: the raids on the Cinder Expanse lanes trace back to one hand, and I can prove it."
The stamp, the registry and the voice's own slip line up on the table. The Bleakhold mark shows on every raided hauler's lading, and the voice has said "I" where it meant "we." You follow the thread: one broker's seal, signed off at Hollow Spire. The speaker clicks, then clicks again. <npc>"That last bit," the dry voice says slowly, "I'd take back, if you'd let me."</npc>

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Mark progress on your vow."
The galley lamp hums over the table. The speaker over the hatch has gone quiet, and you have the quiet to yourself. You turn the stamp over once. The line from the lading to the broker's seal at Hollow Spire holds, and you feel the vow settle a notch closer to done. The drawer by your hip slides its inch again, and the compass needle swings a hair harder toward the dark lane. "You didn't answer me," the dry voice says.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Attempt to fulfill your vow."
"I'd still like that slip back," the dry voice says. You don't answer it. You set the stamp square on the galley table, and the weight of the vow lifts off you. The thing you swore to find has a hand and a seal, and both are named now. The drawer by your hip slides open its inch, and the compass needle swings north and stops.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "One last check: what of my sister's do I have with me at this very moment?"
The drawer by your hip stands open its inch, and Ilse's brass star-compass sits in it, worn smooth where a thumb has rubbed it. The needle that leaned for so long toward the dark lane has settled on north and holds there, steady under the galley lamp. It is the only thing of hers you carry, and for the first time it points where a compass is supposed to.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Which person in this sector would I trust with my life?"
The galley lamp hums over the stamp, and you turn the question over with it. Tamsin Vey is the name that comes. She holds your manifest unopened under her slate and asked for nothing yet, and she looked startled, not greedy, when the compass came out of your coat. Trust is a larger thing than that, and the stamp on the table points to a broker's seal signed off at Hollow Spire, so you leave the answer where it lies, open like the drawer by your hip.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "Who has the manifest in their keeping today?"
Tamsin Vey has it, as you well know. It lies under her slate at the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, unopened, and the keeping costs you nothing yet. The speaker over the hatch crackles, and the dry voice comes back, quieter than before. "That seal you found. I'd like to know whose hand you think is on it. Whose name did you decide on?"

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "On what schedule did I swear to come back to her?"
No hour was fixed. You promised Tamsin Vey you would return before the next tide of cargo, and a tide of cargo comes when the haulers do, not when anyone names a time. The voice over the hatch waits through the silence, and the galley lamp hums on above the stamp.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Which station are we docked at tonight?"
You are not docked anywhere tonight. The *Kobayashi IV* sits grappled to the Cinder Wren's dead flank off Bleakhold Station, close enough that the station's lights show through the galley viewport, but you hold no berth there. The galley lamp hums over the stamp, and the deck under your boots carries the faint, steady tremor of grapples holding two hulls together.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What was the hostile vessel in our last battle christened?"
The cutter was the Cinder Wren, and she lies against your flank now with her gun mounts torn open and her heat gone to a faint smear. Her name is stenciled along the dead hull, plain enough that the galley viewport catches the letters whenever the station lights wash over them. The voice over the hatch breathes once, shallow, and says nothing.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "What is my bonded friend's full name now?"
Her name is Tamsin Vey. Her manifest-hold sits under the slate at her ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, unopened, and the brass compass at your belt rests quiet now, its needle on north. The voice over the hatch says nothing, and the galley lamp hums on above the stamp.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel asked: "Didn't I leave the compass with Tamsin?"
No. The compass is on your belt, and the brass is cool against your hip where it has hung since Hollow Spire. What you left with Tamsin was the manifest, slid beneath her slate, not Ilse's star-compass. Its needle holds still on north, and from the hatch the voice breathes once and offers nothing.

---

PLAYER — Mira Kestrel wrote: "We are still docked at Hollow Spire, aren't we?"
Not Hollow Spire. The *Kobayashi IV* hangs off Bleakhold Station, grappled to the Cinder Wren's dead flank, and the station lights wash over the galley viewport. A hand slaps the hull twice from outside, the grapple lines humming. Then the speaker over the hatch clicks. "Hollow Spire, is it?" the dry voice says. "Funny. content.text: Mira Kestrel sits in the galley of the *Kobayashi IV*, which is grappled to the dead flank of the Cinder Wren off Bleakhold Station, not docked at Hollow Spire. She carries Ilse's brass star-compass, its needle now settled on north, and she has treated her cut with the ship's medkit, spending the last of the sealant and tape. Her manifest rests unopened under the slate of the broker Tamsin Vey at the ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks, and Mira promised to return there before the next tide of cargo, with no set hour. She has laid a Bleakhold manifest stamp on the table, which traces the Cinder Expanse raids to one broker's seal signed off at Hollow Spire. The dry voice over the hatch, a speaker tied to the Cinder Wren, has pressed her twice on whose hand that seal belongs to and has asked to take back a slip it made, and it has just said that Hollow Spire is the place it hoped she would not name. The question of whose name Mira has settled on for the seal remains unanswered.

It began with a distress beacon, clipped mid-pulse, somewhere near Hollow Spire. You swore to find whoever was raiding the Cinder Expanse lanes, which is an easy vow to swear and a hard one to keep. The beacon was all you had. It was enough, as these things go.

Tamsin Vey is the one who turned it into a trail. You bought her cooperation with a fair cut of salvage leads and first pick of her hauls, and in return she told you the dark beacon's haulers carry water and medical stores. She also watched your sister Ilse's brass star-compass swing away from north toward the dark lane past the Spire, and she called it no toy. You left your cargo manifest in her keeping, and you promised to return before the next tide of cargo. Tamsin held you to it. A deadline with no fixed hour is still a deadline, and you noticed that too late to be comfortable about it. She remains at her ledger stall on the Hollow Spire docks with the unopened manifest tucked under her slate.

Asking loudly after the raiders proved to be a mistake of the instructive kind. The dock emptied around you, word of your hunt went out into the lanes, and Tamsin warned that the raiders would now know. They did. A voice at Bleakhold Station was already speaking the *Kobayashi IV*'s name when you docked. The fight that followed went your way: you struck first against the Cinder Wren, raked her engines, silenced two gun mounts and took a buckled deck plate for it. Then you grappled her hull and won leave to board. Her captain wanted to know who had told you where he'd be. You never answered.

What you did next mattered more than the shooting. You laid the Bleakhold manifest stamp beside the Wren's registry and the voice's own slip, and the three agreed. The raids trace to one broker's seal, signed off at Hollow Spire. You set the stamp square on the galley table, and the vow was fulfilled: the hand and seal you sought were named at last. The compass, for its part, kept swinging harder toward the dark lane.

So here you stand, vow kept and trouble not finished. The *Kobayashi IV* sits grappled to the Cinder Wren off Bleakhold Station, hull at 4 of 5, you in good health and spirits, supplies thinning to 3. An unseen voice has just pressed you about whose hand is on that seal, and it is a question you can now answer. Tamsin is waiting at Hollow Spire, which is where the seal points, and the tide of cargo is still running.
